newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb opposition sceptical of Milosevic intentions.
newsitem.headline: Serb opposition sceptical of Milosevic intentions.

text.p: The Serbian opposition voiced scepticism about President Slobodan Milosevic's intentions after parliament approved a special law on Tuesday reinstating opposition victories in local elections, and said its protests will continue.

"On November 18 the president of Serbia decided to steal our votes and spat in the face of all people in Serbia," Vesna Pesic, one of the three opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition leaders, told 60,000 supporters in Belgrade on Tuesday evening.

"The regime is terminally ill but we still face a long uphill struggle. We want full media freedom but I'm afraid we shall be seeing each other for quite some time to achieve that," the Nobel peace prize nominee said.
Pesic is one of three peace activists from former Yugoslavia to be nominated for the Nobel prize by the International Peace Bureau.
Hours earlier, the Serbian parliament passed a special law reinstating opposition election victories in Serbia's 14 biggest cities, including Belgrade.

The ruling Socialists had annulled them on grounds of unspecified "irregularities" -- a move that prompted an international outcry and three months of massive protests by thousands of people venting their anger at the authorities, biased state media and the deteriorating economic situation.
The huge demonstrations opened up cracks in the leftist monolith which had ruled Serbia for 52 years.

Milosevic, facing the biggest challenge in his 10 years in power and rifts within his party and the police over whether to use force, asked the socialist-dominated parliament to approve a bill recognising the opposition victories.
Britain welcomed the Serbian parliament's move but pressed for further democratisation and for liberalisation of the media.

"I welcome the step taken today by the Serbian parliament. The Serbian authorities must now implement this legislation and reinstate opposition victories without further delay," said Sir Nicholas Bonsor, a foreign office minister.
Britain "will continue to encourage further democratisation in Serbia -- including through our support for the independent media", he added.

Zajedno officials fear Milosevic may cut off funding for the towns they control and are wary about his grip on the local media. The media remain probably the single most powerful tool for the elections this year and Milosevic would be reluctant to relinquish control, they said.

"The Socialists are just buying time until the republican and presidential elections. As far as we are concerned, the opposition will have the necessary means to keep fighting on," said Ranko Funjga, a 33-year old Belgrade citizen.
"The real reason for all the different protests going on in Serbia is our bad regime, and nothing essential will change until that regime goes," said Zoran Djindjic, another Zajedno leader .

"They are wrong if they think that our demands are only material -- we want our honour and dignity back, he said. "Serbia must be reformed so it can find its own place under the sun. Our place is on the world market, not in the blind alley into which they are taking us," he added.

Even the ultra-nationalist Radical Party, once closely allied with the socialists, lashed out at Milosevic. "You have passed this law under force. You will see a disaster, you have destroyed everything that could be destroyed," Radical leader Tomislav Nikolic said.
